questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$   

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+{t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k & =c(i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}t=c \\ 2+{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ 1+{t}^{2}=c(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $t=c.$ Substituting $c=t$ into the second equality gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}2+{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{3} \\ 2 & =2{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{3} & =1 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the equation $1+{t}^{2}=c(2t).$
Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =i+(2+{1}^{3})\,j+(1+{1}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+3\,j+2\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $P(1,3,2).$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve  $r(t)=(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+(t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r(\frac{\pi }{2})+u{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find $r(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2})\,i+(\frac{\pi }{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2})\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =(1-1)i+(\frac{\pi }{2}+0)\,j+2\sqrt{2}\,k \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\,j+2\sqrt{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})]\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,i+(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2})\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =-0\,i+(1-1)\,j+\sqrt{2}\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
R(u)=\frac{\pi }{2}\,j+2\sqrt{2}\,k+u(\sqrt{2}\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1,\operatorname{arctan}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=0,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{2}-1,\operatorname{arctan}⁡0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨2(0),\frac{1}{{0}^{2}+1}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2{t}^{3},3{t}^{2}-6t⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1,-4⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}-6t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6{t}^{2},6t-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨1,-4⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1,-4⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,-4⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1,-4⟩\cdot ⟨6{t}^{2},6t-6⟩ & =0 \\ 1(6{t}^{2})+(-4)(6t-6) & =0 \\ 6{t}^{2}-24t+24 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}-4t+4 & =0 \\ (t-2)^{2} & =0 \\ t & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨2(2)^{3},3(2)^{2}-6(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨16,0⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,-4⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(16,0).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=(1-3t)\,i+2\sqrt{t}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-3t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t})\,j \\  & =-3\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [(1-3t)\,i+2\sqrt{t}\,j]\cdot (-3i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,j) & =0 \\ (1-3t)\cdot (-3)+2\sqrt{t}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} & =0 \\ -3+9t+2 & =0 \\ 9t-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=\frac{1}{9}.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{1}{9})=(1-3\cdot \frac{1}{9})\,i+2\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}}\,j=\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$
